title: CBC Interpretation: Start With the Cell Line and Clinical Question
bottomLine: A CBC is not one result. Interpret hemoglobin/hematocrit, leukocytes/differential and platelets as separate cell-line problems, then integrate indices, trends and symptoms before choosing the next test or disposition.
recognize: Anemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia and thrombocytopenia have different differentials and safety implications.
A falling value can matter more than a single mildly abnormal result when bleeding, marrow suppression or sepsis is plausible.
differentiate: Hemoconcentration can raise hemoglobin without increasing red-cell mass; dilution can lower it without true loss.
Neutrophilia, lymphocytosis and eosinophilia are patterns, not standalone diagnoses.
assessment: Assess bleeding, infection, medications, nutrition, pregnancy, kidney/liver disease, malignancy/therapy and baseline trends.
workup: Use red-cell indices, reticulocytes, smear, iron/B12/folate, hemolysis studies or marrow/specialty testing only when they answer the identified cell-line problem.
management: Treat instability first, then the cause. Stable abnormalities require cause-directed follow-up rather than reflex transfusion, antibiotics or hematology referral for every deviation.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants, marrow-suppressive drugs and therapies that alter counts before attributing the result to disease.
counselling: Explain which cell line is abnormal and why a trend or additional test is needed before naming the cause.
followUp: Close the loop on repeat counts and cause-directed testing; urgent abnormalities require same-day escalation.
examTrap: Treating 'abnormal CBC' as one diagnosis instead of identifying which cell line is driving the risk.
oneLinePearl: CBC reasoning starts with the cell line, then the trend, then the cause.

title: Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Interpret the Pattern, Not the Printout
bottomLine: A broad chemistry panel combines electrolytes, renal markers, glucose and liver-related analytes that answer different questions. Identify the dangerous abnormality first, then determine whether the pattern reflects volume status, organ dysfunction, medication effect or a chronic baseline before ordering more tests.
recognize: Potassium, sodium, glucose, creatinine and bicarbonate can create immediate safety issues; mild isolated abnormalities often require context and confirmation.
A single creatinine or liver enzyme result does not define chronic kidney or liver disease.
differentiate: Volume depletion, medication effects and acute illness can shift several chemistry values together.
Transaminases indicate injury, not synthetic liver function; creatinine is an imperfect filtration surrogate.
assessment: Assess symptoms, hydration/perfusion, medications, renal/liver history, diabetes, GI losses, diet/supplements and baseline laboratory values.
workup: Repeat/confirm clinically important unexpected results and use focused urine, endocrine, acid-base or imaging studies only when the pattern justifies them.
management: Treat life-threatening electrolyte/glucose/acid-base disturbances immediately while investigating cause; stable chronic patterns need longitudinal disease management.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs/MRAs, diuretics, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors and many other drugs can materially change chemistry values and risk.
counselling: Explain that the panel is a collection of clues, not a single pass/fail test.
followUp: Trend only the values that answer a defined clinical question and act on deterioration promptly.
examTrap: Ordering a second broad panel instead of addressing the one dangerous abnormality already visible.
oneLinePearl: On a chemistry panel, prioritize what can harm the patient now, then explain the pattern.

title: Lipid Panel Interpretation: Convert Numbers Into Cardiovascular Risk Decisions
bottomLine: Interpret lipids in the context of established ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, familial hypercholesterolemia risk and overall cardiovascular risk. The treatment decision is not simply 'LDL high = statin' or 'LDL normal = no risk'.
recognize: Established ASCVD and other high-risk conditions can indicate lipid-lowering therapy even when one lipid value is not dramatic.
Marked triglyceride elevation raises a different immediate concern than isolated LDL elevation.
differentiate: Primary prevention and secondary prevention use different thresholds/intensity logic.
Unexpected severe dyslipidemia should prompt review of secondary causes and familial disease.
assessment: Assess smoking, BP, diabetes, kidney disease, premature family history, prior vascular disease, pregnancy plans and medications.
workup: Use fasting testing selectively when triglycerides or a specific calculation/question requires it; investigate secondary causes when the pattern is severe or unexpected.
management: Use current Canadian cardiovascular-risk guidance to select treatment intensity and follow response/adherence after therapy changes.
medicationSafety: Review statin interactions, muscle/hepatic symptoms when clinically indicated and pregnancy-specific medication decisions.
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular risk and expected treatment benefit rather than focusing only on a target number.
followUp: Repeat lipids at a clinically useful interval after initiation/intensification and reassess adherence/tolerance.
examTrap: Treating the lipid panel without first identifying whether the patient is primary or secondary prevention.
oneLinePearl: A lipid panel refines cardiovascular risk; it does not replace risk stratification.

title: Thyroid Function Tests: Know When TSH Is Trustworthy
bottomLine: TSH is the preferred first-line test for most suspected primary thyroid disease, but central/pituitary disease, pregnancy, severe non-thyroidal illness and assay/medication interference can make TSH alone misleading. Interpret TSH with free T4 when the clinical context requires it.
recognize: High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; suppressed TSH with elevated free hormone supports primary hyperthyroidism.
Low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH raises central hypothyroidism concern.
differentiate: Biotin and selected medications can distort assays; acute illness can create non-thyroidal patterns without true primary thyroid disease.
Free T3 is rarely the first test for uncomplicated suspected hypothyroidism.
assessment: Review symptoms, pregnancy, pituitary symptoms, amiodarone/lithium, supplements/biotin, thyroid medication timing/adherence and recent severe illness.
workup: Use TSH first when the pituitary axis is intact, adding free T4 and cause-directed antibodies/imaging only when indicated.
management: Treat confirmed disease and repeat testing after physiologically meaningful intervals rather than reacting to values before steady state.
medicationSafety: Levothyroxine absorption/interactions and antithyroid-drug toxicity can confound follow-up interpretation.
counselling: Explain why thyroid tests may need repeat/paired interpretation rather than one result deciding treatment.
followUp: Recheck according to treatment change, pregnancy and disease context; avoid unnecessary repeated panels.
examTrap: Using a normal TSH to exclude hypothyroidism in a patient with suspected pituitary disease and low free T4.
oneLinePearl: TSH leads in primary thyroid disease; free T4 rescues you when the pituitary context changes.

title: Liver Enzyme Pattern Recognition: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Risk
bottomLine: Classify liver chemistry as predominantly hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed before choosing the differential. AST/ALT reflect injury, alkaline phosphatase supports cholestasis after source confirmation, and INR/albumin/bilirubin answer different questions about function and handling.
recognize: Predominant aminotransferase elevation suggests hepatocellular injury; predominant alkaline-phosphatase elevation suggests cholestatic/infiltrative disease.
Falling AST/ALT can be falsely reassuring in severe acute liver injury if INR, bilirubin, glucose or mental status worsen.
differentiate: ALP may be bone/placental rather than hepatic; albumin is affected by inflammation/nutrition/renal loss.
Bilirubin can rise in both hepatocellular and cholestatic disease and should be interpreted by fraction and pattern.
assessment: Assess jaundice, pruritus, pain, fever, encephalopathy, bleeding, alcohol, medications/supplements, pregnancy and infectious/metabolic risks.
workup: Use cause-directed viral/toxic/metabolic/autoimmune testing and ultrasound when the pattern warrants it rather than ordering every liver test for every mild abnormality.
management: Treat the cause and escalate suspected acute liver failure, cholangitis or rapidly progressive disease.
medicationSafety: Do not stop or restart essential potentially hepatotoxic medications solely from one small enzyme change without risk-benefit review and the full pattern.
counselling: Explain that liver enzymes show injury pattern, not a direct percentage of liver function.
followUp: Trend abnormalities that answer a clinical question and refer persistent/progressive unexplained disease appropriately.
examTrap: Calling aminotransferase elevation 'liver failure' without assessing synthetic function and clinical status.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow and synthetic function are different axes.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Myocardial Injury Is Not Automatically Myocardial Infarction
bottomLine: High-sensitivity troponin identifies myocardial injury; myocardial infarction requires injury plus compatible ischemic evidence. Interpret serial change, timing, symptoms and ECG together, and use BNP/NT-proBNP as heart-failure probability/risk tools rather than stand-alone diagnoses.
recognize: Troponin can rise with ACS, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmia, PE, sepsis, renal disease and other myocardial stress.
BNP/NT-proBNP is influenced by age, renal function, obesity and atrial fibrillation.
differentiate: A normal early troponin does not automatically exclude early ACS; a chronically elevated troponin does not automatically equal acute MI.
CK-MB is generally lower value than modern troponin for routine ACS diagnosis.
assessment: Assess symptom timing, ECG, hemodynamics, renal function, heart-failure signs and alternate causes of myocardial injury.
workup: Use the validated local serial high-sensitivity troponin pathway and additional imaging/testing based on ischemic probability and alternate diagnoses.
management: Activate ACS/acute-care pathways when clinical/ECG/serial biomarker evidence supports ischemia; treat alternate causes of myocardial injury when they are more likely.
medicationSafety: Do not give antithrombotic therapy solely for a troponin elevation before considering bleeding risk and alternative diagnoses such as aortic syndrome.
redFlags: Rising troponin with ongoing ischemic symptoms
counselling: Explain why repeat testing may be required even when the first marker is normal or mildly elevated.
followUp: Close pending serial markers and ensure the cause of myocardial injury is documented and managed.
examTrap: Calling every elevated troponin an NSTEMI without ischemic evidence.
oneLinePearl: Troponin says injury; the clinical syndrome says why.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society acute coronary syndrome and heart failure guidance

title: Tumor Markers: Use Them for the Right Cancer Question
bottomLine: Most serum tumor markers are not population screening tests and are rarely diagnostic by themselves. Use a marker only when a validated cancer-specific question exists—such as treatment response, recurrence surveillance or selected diagnostic support—and interpret it with imaging, pathology and clinical context.
recognize: Markers can be elevated by benign disease and can remain normal despite cancer.
The useful marker and threshold depend on the cancer type, treatment state and clinical question.
differentiate: Screening an asymptomatic average-risk population is different from monitoring a known malignancy.
A rising marker can trigger evaluation but does not independently prove recurrence or progression.
assessment: Clarify whether the patient has a known cancer, symptoms, high-risk genetic syndrome or a defined specialty monitoring plan before ordering a marker.
workup: Use cancer-specific guideline pathways and confirm clinically important changes with appropriate imaging/pathology rather than serial marker testing alone.
management: Refer suspicious cancer presentations through the appropriate diagnostic pathway; do not reassure or treat solely on marker status.
medicationSafety: Avoid invasive procedures or therapy changes based only on a nonspecific marker without confirmatory evaluation.
redFlags: Cancer alarm symptoms with a 'normal' marker
Rapid unexplained marker rise in known cancer
New organ dysfunction suggesting metastatic disease
counselling: Explain that tumor markers are imperfect and are usually used as one part of cancer monitoring, not as a universal cancer blood test.
followUp: Track any abnormal marker within the cancer-specific diagnostic or surveillance plan and document who owns follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering a broad panel of tumor markers to screen an asymptomatic patient for hidden cancer.
oneLinePearl: A tumor marker needs a validated cancer question before it needs a blood draw.
sourceBasis: Canadian cancer-specific diagnostic and surveillance practice

title: Inflammatory Markers: Move Probability, Do Not Name the Disease
bottomLine: CRP and ESR are nonspecific. Use them when a defined clinical question exists and when the result can change probability, urgency or follow-up; do not use an elevated value as proof of bacterial infection, autoimmune disease or occult cancer.
recognize: CRP changes more rapidly and is generally preferable for acute systemic inflammation; ESR is slower and more confounded by age, anemia, pregnancy and proteins.
Discordant markers can occur and should be interpreted through the disease context rather than normalized by ordering more nonspecific tests.
differentiate: Normal markers do not safely exclude time-critical disease when the clinical syndrome is compelling.
Selected diseases such as giant-cell arteritis use inflammatory markers as supporting evidence, not as the sole diagnostic criterion.
assessment: Define the suspected syndrome, pretest probability and the management decision that a high/low result would change.
workup: Use disease-specific tests, cultures/imaging or specialist evaluation when indicated rather than repeated CRP/ESR without a diagnostic hypothesis.
management: Treat the clinical diagnosis and patient severity; trend markers only when the trajectory has a validated role in management.
medicationSafety: Do not start/broaden antibiotics or immunosuppression solely because a nonspecific inflammatory marker is elevated.
redFlags: Clinical sepsis/organ dysfunction despite low marker
Visual symptoms with possible giant-cell arteritis
Persistent systemic illness/weight loss requiring definitive evaluation
counselling: Explain that inflammatory markers indicate inflammation but usually cannot tell the exact cause.
followUp: Stop trending when the result no longer changes care and reassess diagnosis when marker and clinical course diverge.
examTrap: Diagnosing bacterial infection from an elevated CRP without a compatible syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory markers adjust probability; they do not finish the differential.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Biochemistry recommendations
